paragraphs.text: By a basket of summer fruit is showed the near approach of Israel’s end, Amo 8:1-3. Their oppression of the poor shall cause their joy to be turned into mourning, Amo 8:4-10. A famine of God’s word threatened, Amo 8:11-14.
see Amo 7:1,4,7.
paragraphs.anchor: Thus hath the Lord God showed unto me: and behold

paragraphs.text: a hook, say some, with which the gatherer might either pull down the bough, or pull off the ripe fruit; or a basket into which the ripe fruit gathered was put to be carried away.
not the early ripe fruit, but that which, as it needed, so had the whole summer’s heat to ripen it, and was gathered in at the end of the summer.
the like question you have Amo 7:8, which see.
see Amo 8:1. Then said the Lord unto me: the meaning of this hieroglyphic not being very plain in itself, the Lord doth here explain it in the following words.
of God’s patience towards Israel, of their peace, growth, and glory; the end of their ripening, they are now as fruit fully ripe, in the end of the year, fit to be gathered.
so they were once, so they boast themselves, so the nations about them account Israel to be the people of God.
see Amo 7:8. God had with admirable patience spared and tried, but now he will with just severity punish, neither pardon nor spare.
paragraphs.anchor: I will not again pass by them any more

paragraphs.text: which were composed by choicest wits, and set to sweetest tunes, and chanted out by most skilful singers to the best musical instruments.

either to take in Judah, and foretell the desolation of their temple; or else, by an irony, the idol temples; or else of the palace, as the word in the Hebrew. All court mirth and jollity, balls and music entertainments.
Heb. shall howl; be turned into the hideous out cries of undone and despairing men.

when God shall execute his judgments threatened, as he did begin on the death of Jeroboam, and continued that day of vengeance till Shalmaneser finished the work in the ruin of Samaria and its captivity.
this is added to assure Israel that what Amos did foretell should be accomplished, for God spake it.

so there were when Shallum slew Zachariah, so there were when Menahem slew Shallum, when he came with his army against Samaria, when he ripped up the women with child in Tiphsah, 2Ki 15:16, and when other usurpers pressed through blood and treason to the crown; beside the howlings when Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser cruelly wasted all.
paragraphs.anchor: There shall be many dead bodies

paragraphs.text: in cities, towns, and country, in palaces and temples too, in all which the bloody effects of enemies’ swords, the wastes of famine and pestilence, should be seen.
who howl, who see this,

either shall secretly bury them, so some, or, to rid themselves of that trouble, shall cast them out wherever they can, with silence, that none may observe them; so great calamitous mortality, that the living suffice not to bury the dead; or so great cruelty by the enemy used against them, that they dare not bury them, or if they do, it must be undiscerned: see Amo 6:10.
paragraphs.anchor: shall cast them forth with silence

paragraphs.text: Though the prophet had several times told them what were the sins for which God would thus punish Israel, yet on a repeated threat he repeateth the rehearsal of the sins which draw down these judgments on their heads.
attend, and consider it,
greedily and cruelly devour, that do, like the greater fish, swallow up the lesser fry: in this one word the prophet includeth all the methods of their cruel oppression, wasting tho poor.
such as were objects of your mercy, had you been just and honest, as well as rich and great.
either to root them out, or to enslave them, while their necessities force them to sell themselves for bread.
paragraphs.anchor: Even to make the poor of the land to fail

paragraphs.text: ye that could wish there were nothing to interrupt your marketing, your irreligious impatience, and your eagerness after the world, look on solemn times of Divine worship as very burdensome; such was the first day of every month, and the weekly sabbath.
paragraphs.anchor: When will the new moon be gone?

paragraphs.text: no servile work might be done on new moons, no markets kept, or corn brought forth publicly to be sold.

they were also bound very religiously to observe the sabbath, and on that day they might not buy or sell; now they are weary of the sabbath, as of the new moon, and on the same account wish it over: here was irreligious gaping after gain.
paragraphs.anchor: And the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat?

paragraphs.text: the ephah was a measure for dry things, and contained about half a bushel and one pottle English measure. Now these covetous corn-merchants measured the corn they sold by an ephah that was too little, the poor buyer had not his due.

they weighed the money which they received, and these rich men had no more pity and justice, than to make their shekel weight greater than the standard; so the poor were twice oppressed in the same way, had less than was their right, and paid more than they ought to pay; and thus they undid the poor, and ate him up.
deceitfully pervert the balances, that the money or shekel weighed, though of full weight, yet appeared too light on the balance, and they who paid it were forced to add more silver to it.
paragraphs.anchor: And falsifying the balances by deceit

paragraphs.text: either it speaks the aim of these men in oppressing the poor thus, that they might at last buy their persons for servants and drudges, or else it speaks the reason why they would have new moons and sabbaths over, that they might to market to buy the poor.
i.e. a little silver, at under value, as Amo 2:6.

this explains the former, and shows us that these cruel oppressors lay in wait for the needy to buy them for a very trifle; when these poor owed but for a very little and cheap commodity, as suppose a pair of shoes, these merciless men would take the advantage against them. and make them sell themselves to pay the debt. All which practices are most directly against the law of God.
paragraphs.anchor: The needy for a pair of shoes

paragraphs.text: that which is fitter for hogs to month, or for horses to eat, the poor must either buy at dear rate or starve; and this another kind of oppression, corrupted wares at excessive rates, sold to those that were necessitous.

who changeth not, whose words and purposes are immutably true and stedfast, who hath often told you, that unless you repent he will punish for your sins, now he hath sworn it, and sends you word by me, that he hath in most solemn and irrevocable manner determined, published, and expressly declared that he will visit all your sins upon you.
by himself, for God cannot swear by any greater, and he is called the excellency of Jacob, Psa 47:4.
Heb. If; if I am a God, I will remember and punish.
or let pass unpunished; I will never remit the punishment by an act of pardon, nor ever omit to punish by an act of forgetfulness.
not one of all those their abominable injustices and irreligion, not one of these cruelties.
either literally, are not such sins and judgments enough to shake the very foundations of the earth? Or, metonymically, the land for the people of it, as after in the verse, they that dwell therein.
this that you have done, O house of Israel, in sinning, and this that God will do in punishing, enough to melt the earth, as Psa 46:6.
since every one hath sinned too much, and every one shall suffer in this approaching calamity, every one at the news may well mourn and lament;
in the land of Israel.

or, by an interrogation, shall it not? i.e. shall not the judgment, the invading troops of Assyria, the displeasure of God, rise and grow as a mighty, wasting flood? or else thus, the whole land shall rise up; soaked in these judgments, it shall seem to swell and grow greater, ready, like a hydropic, to burst asunder: or else it is a hypallage, the land shall rise up, i.e. the flood shall rise over the land; or, which I rather incline to, the whole judgment shall rise as a flood.
paragraphs.anchor: It shall rise up wholly as a flood

paragraphs.text: the land, the state, people, and what they have, shall be, as in a shipwreck, or mighty flood which breaks all down before it, tossed in the surges and waves;
and at last, by the continuance of this tempest, drowned all as the overflowing on Nilus doth drown all the plains of Egypt.
paragraphs.anchor: and drowned as by the flood of Egypt

paragraphs.text: most certainly it will be,
when God begins to execute these his just and severe judgments on the ten tribes.
the great, just, holy, and terrible God, who is provoked by these sins, and hath denounced these judgments, my hand shall be evident in it.

literally, say some, but erroneously; by sun I understand rather the settled state of their prosperity under their present government in the house of Jehu; or it may refer particularly to their king and court, which Jeroboam at his death left like the sun at noon in the height of their glory, as all know who know the history of those times.

so Israel’s sun did as at noon set under the dark cloud of home-bred conspiracies and civil wars by Shallum, Menahem, Pekah, and Hoshea, till the midnight darkness drew on by Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser.
bring a thick cloud of troubles and afflictions.

the common people, the whole body of the nation; so the sun speaks the royalty, nobility, and great ones of this kingdom, by an allusion well known in Scripture, and the earth speaks the common sort of people; and all are here threatened.
when they did think (as in Jeroboam’s time) all was safe, sure, and well settled, far from the night of sorrow and trouble, then will God bring all this he threateneth upon them.
religious, though idolatrous in your temples, see Amo 8:3, and your ordinary civil feasts in your palaces, into mourning: see Amo 8:3.
this ingemination doth assure the thing, and forebode the sadness of their state.
paragraphs.anchor: And all your songs into lamentation

paragraphs.text: as all inwardly shall be sadness, so all that appears outwardly shall speak their sorrow and sadness.
all sorts of persons should put on this mourning, and gird it close to their loins that it might afflict them the more, a custom very general in those times and places.
partly pulling off the hair of the head through anguish, or shaving the head and beard in sign of greatest sadness, as the Eastern people did: see Mic 1:16.

this is accounted the greatest mourning, and seems proverbially to express such mourning, Jer 6:26 Zec 12:10, which see; so God will afflict this people with greatest sorrows, and fill them with greatest mourning.
paragraphs.anchor: As the mourning of an only son

paragraphs.text: you may hope these troubles will be over, and come to an end, but that will be little to your comfort; a bitter day, which you shall wish you had never seen, shall succeed your dark night, as indeed it doth to this day.
note well what now I shall declare to you, and consider it.
surely, speedily, and according to the threats of God.
paragraphs.anchor: The days come, saith the Lord God

paragraphs.text: by a signal hand of Divine displeasure it shall appear to be from God, that such a famine cometh upon them of Israel.
paragraphs.anchor: I will send a famine in the land

paragraphs.text: a spiritual famine joined with a corporal famine; their bodies were pined with famine, destitute of bread and water; and this God sent too. but the famine of the soul is worse and more grievous.
paragraphs.anchor: Not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water

paragraphs.text: either the written word which Israel had among them till their captivity, but afterwards should ever want both it and those who should interpret it to them, or else the word of prophecy; now they despise it, though they have it, but then they shall desire it, and have it not. They shall hunt after prophets, to tell them when their troubles shall end, though now they hate prophets who warn them, that their troubles might not begin: now Israel despiseth a prophet’s counsel, then they shall hunt for it, but not have a prophet to give them counsel, as Psa 74:9.
search all places for a prophet or a preacher from the Syrian or Midland Sea to that of Tiberias, to the Dead Sea, and to the Red Sea.
paragraphs.anchor: They shall wander from sea to sea

paragraphs.text: that mountainous tract whither persecuted Elijah fled, and perhaps other prophets in like circumstances retired; proverbially, they shall search all corners for a prophet.
paragraphs.anchor: From the north even to the east

paragraphs.text: shall diligently and speedily, on every report that a prophet is, on hearsays, in such or such a place, hasten thither, as Ahab in his search for Elijah, 1Ki 18:10.
paragraphs.anchor: They shall run to and fro

paragraphs.text: hoping to hear some good news of an end of their miseries from God by a prophet.
paragraphs.anchor: To seek the word of the Lord

paragraphs.text: they persecuted and slew such as foretold the beginning of this misery, and now it is come they shall neither hear the news nor see the hopes of an end. God did tell them it would be utter ruin, and no prophet of God can tell them any better news.

It is probable these in their strength and rigour would seek earnestly to know what end they might expect, whether they should outlive this famine of the word, and the famine of bread and water, but both should faint with thirst and hunger; neither finding the word of the Lord for their comfort, they should faint with despair, nor finding bread and water, should faint and die with weakness: so Israel should be extinguished.
who now do, as formerly they have done, trust in, sacrifice to, and swear by; who are obstinate idolaters, and trust to those lies.
that which was the sin, the occasion of the sin,
the calves at Dan and Beth-el.
think, profess, and swear too,
the idol at Dan is the true and living God.
the idols at, Beer-sheba, to which the zealous, mad, and bigoted idolaters in Israel made their pilgrimages.
be consumed by famine, sword, and captivity,
never return out of captivity, nor recover of this consumption.
